RagShortTexts: The House of Montfort combined crusader religious piety with revolutionary parliamentary.

Variants.Content: The Montfort arms, a silver lion with a forked tail on red, appeared on the banners of a family that produced crusaders and statesmen whose careers ran across France, Italy, and England. Amaury de Montfort led crusade forces in the Albigensian wars, and the family's piety shaped its politics for generations. Simon de Montfort, sixth Earl of Leicester, married Eleanor, the sister of King Henry III, in 1238. He then led the baronial rebellion against Henry's government, pressing the Provisions of Oxford and reform of royal finance. In 1265 he summoned knights and burgesses to a great parliament, a step that set a precedent for representative assemblies in England. His death at Evesham in 1265 ended his rule, but the precedent remained.

Montfort combined intense ascetic piety with baronial constitutionalism. Critics called him an ambitious demagogue who used the reform program to strip the king of his rightful powers, while reformers hailed him as the champion of lawful liberties. His letters to the shire courts and town councils were copied and read aloud.
Commoners hail 'Righteous Simon' across London and Oxford. Elevating merchant guild aldermen to royal councils created a precedent that permanently altered English feudalism.
